test.llm_feedback:
Summary. You have the right overarching idea: rewrite the hypothesis in complex-exponential form and use the fact that three unit vectors summing to zero must be 120° apart, then double the angles to get the same cancellation. However the write‑up contains several unjustified claims and a few incorrect/sloppy statements that need correction to be a complete argument.

What you did well
- You immediately saw that cos a + i sin a = e^{ia} is the natural way to encode the two real equations as the single complex equation e^{ia}+e^{ib}+e^{ic}=0.
- You reached the correct conclusion e^{i2a}+e^{i2b}+e^{i2c}=0 (and hence the two real doubled-angle sums vanish).

Errors and gaps (how to fix them)
1. Confusion between angles and their affixes. You wrote “a, b, c are affixes … (a + b + c)/3 = 0.” This is incorrect: the complex points (affixes) are e^{ia}, e^{ib}, e^{ic}, not a,b,c themselves. If you want to talk about a centroid you must use (e^{ia}+e^{ib}+e^{ic})/3 = 0 (which is just restating the hypothesis), not (a+b+c)/3 = 0.

2. Unjustified jump to a specific rotation. You wrote e^{ia}(1 + e^{i2π/3} + e^{i4π/3}) = 0 without showing why b = a + 2π/3 and c = a + 4π/3 (mod 2π). That is the crucial step that needs justification. A standard rigorous route is: multiply your equation by e^{-ia} to get 1 + e^{i(b-a)} + e^{i(c-a)} = 0, then take the squared modulus (or appeal to the geometry of unit vectors) to deduce that the differences b-a and c-a are separated by ±2π/3 (i.e. the three unit vectors are 120° apart). Include that calculation or geometric argument—without it the claim is unsupported.

3. Sloppy algebra / typos. The “squaring this identity” part is confusing and contains typographical errors (you repeat e^{i2π/3} twice) and an unclear motivation: squaring the zero-sum is not the clearest route. It is better to take e^{-ia}(e^{ia}+e^{ib}+e^{ic}) = 0 and then take modulus squared of 1 + e^{i(b-a)} + e^{i(c-a)} to extract angle information. If you do manipulate exponents, keep track of mod 2π issues and justify why you may replace b by a+2π/3 etc.

4. Modulo 2π remark omitted. When you deduce that the differences are ±2π/3 you should note that this is modulo 2π; that is why one can write (up to rotation) the triple of arguments as {0, 2π/3, 4π/3}. This is a small but important precision.

How to complete the solution succinctly
- Start from e^{ia}+e^{ib}+e^{ic}=0. Multiply by e^{-ia} to get 1 + e^{i(b-a)} + e^{i(c-a)} = 0.
- Take the squared modulus of that equation (or use the geometric vector picture) to conclude the three unit vectors are 120° apart, i.e. b-a and c-a are congruent to 2π/3 and 4π/3 in some order.
- Therefore (mod 2π) b = a + 2π/3, c = a + 4π/3 (up to permutation). Doubling those congruences keeps the 120° spacing, so e^{i2a}+e^{i2b}+e^{i2c}=0, which gives the required real and imaginary sums of cos2· and sin2· equal to zero.

Final remark
Your intuition and final conclusion are correct; tighten the argument by (i) not mixing angles with their complex exponentials, (ii) giving the modulus-squared or geometric justification for the 120° spacing, and (iii) cleaning up the algebra/notation (avoid squaring the zero-sum in an opaque way). With those fixes the solution would be complete and rigorous.

test.prompt:
\ $N(>2)$ dogs are equidistantly distributed on the circumference of a circle of radius $R$. Suddenly, at $t = 0$, the dogs enter a race where each chases his nearest (counter-clockwise) neighbour. Assume that for $t > 0$ each dog runs at a constant speed $v$ at a heading always directly towards its neighbour.
Will the dogs ever catch up with each other? If so, what distance will they traverse before
doing so?
test.output:
\begin{proof}
Due to the dogs being equidistant from each other, we use the symmetry principle to determine that the position of the dogs will form an equilateral triangle of which the center will be the center of the original circle since the dogs will stay equidistant due to symmetry and distance from the center will be the same for all the dogs. \\
From this, we see the dogs will meet at the center if they do indeed meet. We now only need to consider the distance each dog is from the center. \\
Since each dog is travelling at speed $v$ towards each other, we take the component of speed in the direction of the center. \\
Due to results from Trigonometry, this is $\frac{v \sqrt{3}}{2} $.
Our speed is constant, so time until dogs reach the center is $\frac{2R}{v \sqrt{3}}$
\end{proof}
test.feedback: Elements of a correct solution are there, i.e. the notion that symmetry properties of the problem allow us to conclude that the configuration of the $N$ dogs will always be a regular $N$-gon and that describing the motion in polar coordinates shows that the $N$-gon shrinks at a constant rate dependent only on the angular separation of the dogs and speed (hence only on $N$ and $v$), showing both convergence to the center and time/distance to convergence. However, these arguments are not clearly laid out in the proposed solution and the solution only treats the case $N=3$.
test.markscheme: 0/5: No relevant work towards the pursuit problem (e.g. unrelated calculations, no use of symmetry or of components of velocity). 1/5: A few correct observations (for example: the dogs spiral inwards, or “they meet at the centre”) but no valid computation; or an attempt to use symmetry without any quantitative derivation of the radial velocity component. 2/5: The right idea is present (use rotational symmetry so the configuration remains a shrinking regular N‑gon and all dogs have identical motion) but the candidate makes major errors in computing the radial component of velocity or in integrating it (for example wrong angle or sign), or uses non‑trivial steps without justification. 3/5: A correct approach is given and the radial equation dr/dt = −v sin(π/N) is stated or derived but with gaps or imprecise justification (e.g. the geometric argument for the constant angle between the velocity and the inward radius is sketched rather than proved); the integration to get T = R/(v sin(π/N)) and the path length vT = R/sin(π/N) is carried out but some logical steps are omitted. 4/5: A correct and essentially complete solution: one shows by symmetry that the dogs remain at the vertices of a shrinking regular N‑gon, computes the constant angle (using e.g. the chord identity e^{iα}−1 = 2i sin(α/2) e^{i(α/2)}) to obtain dr/dt = −v sin(π/N), integrates to get T = R/(v sin(π/N)) and hence each dog traverses distance R/sin(π/N); only minor omissions or terse justification are allowed. 5/5: Rigorous, well structured solution with explicit justification that the regularity is preserved for t>0, a clear derivation of the angle between the velocity and the inward radial direction and thus dr/dt = −v sin(π/N), correct integration giving T = R/(v sin(π/N)) and path length R/sin(π/N), and a clear concluding statement that the dogs meet at the centre. Note: in awarding marks, correctness and mathematical rigor of the argument are given priority over presentation, notation or stylistic clarity.
test.llm_feedback:
You used the right qualitative idea (symmetry ⇒ the dogs remain at the vertices of a shrinking regular N‑gon and will meet at the centre), but the solution contains a key mistake and some omissions.

Specific comments and how to fix them
- Incorrect specialization to an equilateral triangle: you assumed the dogs form an equilateral triangle and used √3/2 for the radial component. That is only correct when N = 3. The problem is for general N > 2, so you must keep N as a parameter rather than fixing N = 3.
- Missing justification for the radial component: you wrote “due to results from Trigonometry” without showing why the velocity vector makes the angle you quoted with the inward radial. A brief geometric/complex‑number argument (or the chord identity) shows that the angle between the velocity (direction toward the next dog) and the inward radial is π/2 − π/N, so the inward radial component of the speed is v cos(π/2 − π/N) = v sin(π/N). State or justify this step.
- Missing path length: you computed a time (and for the wrong N), but did not state the distance each dog runs. Integrating dr/dt gives the meeting time T and multiplying by v gives the path length; include both.

How to present a complete answer (outline, not a full rewrite)
- State clearly that symmetry implies the configuration stays a regular N‑gon shrinking homothetically, so all radii r(t) are equal.
- Show the angle between the velocity (toward the next dog) and the inward radius is π/2 − π/N and hence dr/dt = −v sin(π/N).
- Integrate from r(0)=R to r(T)=0 to obtain T = R/(v sin(π/N)), and then the distance run by each dog is vT = R/sin(π/N).
- A short remark that the centre is the meeting point completes the argument.

Overall: you picked up the right symmetry idea but made a major error in computing the radial component (by implicitly taking N=3) and omitted the final path length. Fix those points and add the brief geometric justification for the angle between the velocity and the radial to make the solution complete.

test.feedback: The solution correctly begins to set up the problem as an ODE in polar coordinates. However, when doing so, an error in calculation causes a factor $-r$ to be dropped from the final ODE, which then leads to a wrong and simpler closed solution.
test.markscheme: 0/5: No relevant progress (e.g. unrelated mechanics, no use of the polygonal symmetry or polar coordinates). 1/5: Aware of the regular N‑gon symmetry or that a polar description is natural, or an attempt to write velocity components, but the argument is invalid (wrong geometric angle, incorrect decomposition of velocity, or unjustified sign errors). 2/5: The right approach is used (place the dogs at the vertices of a shrinking regular N‑gon, switch to polar coordinates about the center, identify the neighbour angle α = 2π/N), but substantial mistakes remain — for example the direction of the velocity is miscomputed, dr/dt and dθ/dt are found incorrectly, or an algebraic/integration step is missing or unjustified. 3/5: The solver correctly identifies that the velocity points toward the neighbour and decomposes it into radial and tangential components to obtain dr/dt = −v sin(α/2) and dθ/dt = v cos(α/2)/r (or an equivalent pair), then combines them to get the separable ODE dr/dθ = −r tan(α/2), but leaves gaps in justification, skips the constant of integration or does not clearly apply the initial condition r(θ0)=R. 4/5: A correct derivation with only minor slips: the student writes and integrates dr/r = −tan(π/N) dθ to obtain the logarithmic spiral, handles the constant almost correctly but may omit an explicit statement of θ0, or has a small sign/notation slip that does not change the qualitative answer. 5/5: Fully rigorous solution: exploit symmetry, set α = 2π/N, compute the exact angle between the velocity and the inward radial direction, obtain dr/dt = −v sin(α/2) and dθ/dt = v cos(α/2)/r, derive dr/dθ = −r tan(α/2), integrate and apply r(θ0)=R to produce the family of logarithmic spirals r(θ) = R exp(−(θ−θ0) tan(π/N)), and (optionally) note that the dogs meet at the centre in finite time t = R/(v sin(π/N)). Rigor and correctness of the geometric derivation and differential‑equation steps are given priority in grading; stylistic clarity and tidy notation are helpful but secondary, and minor notational sloppiness will not outweigh mathematical errors.
test.llm_feedback:
Summary — what you did well
- You correctly exploited the regular‑N symmetry and switched to polar coordinates about the centre.
- You identified the radial and tangential components of the dog’s velocity as involving the sin(π/N) and cos(π/N) factors — that basic geometric decomposition is the right idea.

Main error (and why it matters)
- The angular speed was written as ˙θ = v cos(π/N). This is dimensionally and physically incorrect because the tangential component of velocity is v_tan = r ˙θ, not ˙θ itself. Equivalently, the tangential speed around the circle of instantaneous radius r equals r times the angular speed. Omitting this factor of r turns a multiplicative dependence on r into a constant, which is why you obtained dr/dθ = −tan(π/N) (a constant) rather than the correct separable ODE where dr/dθ is proportional to r. That mistake changes the qualitative type of trajectory (straight line in your answer) rather than the correct logarithmic spiral.

How to fix it (guidance, not a full re-solution)
- Use v_radial = −v sin(π/N) and v_tangential = v cos(π/N) with v_tangential = r ˙θ. Thus ˙θ = v cos(π/N)/r.
- Form ˙r/˙θ = (−v sin(π/N))/(v cos(π/N)/r) to obtain a separable ODE of the form dr/dθ = −r tan(π/N).
- Integrate this separable ODE and apply the initial condition r(θ0)=R to fix the integration constant. The trajectories are logarithmic spirals (not linear in θ). Also check the time to collision can be obtained from the radial ODE.

Minor remarks
- Keep track of signs and your θ convention (inward radial velocity is negative, and whether θ increases or decreases depends on your orientation). You used the right sign for ˙r but inconsistent handling of ˙θ produced the main error.
- It’s good to state explicitly the neighbour angle α = 2π/N (you used π/N implicitly); being explicit helps avoid off‑by‑2 errors.

Overall
- The approach and geometric decomposition are essentially correct, but a crucial factor r was omitted in the angular component. Fixing that gives the separable ODE dr/dθ = −r tan(π/N), whose integration yields the logarithmic spiral family satisfying r(θ0)=R.
